items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: In fact we made a video and a book called The Mighty Two. You know about that one? It’s Gene Krupa and myself. I went up to his house in Yonkers and spent a week with him.

ctx.x: We were talking about your career as an author and working in the field of the education of music. I have a book that I don’t know if you were familiar with coming up. I found these probably about 20 years ago in a used book store. It’s called The Science of Drumming, book 1 and 2, by Gene Krupa. Are you familiar with either – with this book?

Yes I am. Gene was another example of a guy that didn’t read too much. I didn’t know that. I thought he was well schooled, even though he studied something with Roy Knapp, but he had problems with reading too. In fact we made a video and a book called The Mighty Two. You know about that one? It’s Gene Krupa and myself. I went up to his house in Yonkers and spent a week with him. We did all the rudiments to swing time. The band was – Ron Carter was the bass player. Barry Harris was the piano player. Phil Wood was…
Sam Rowland? Edited by Sam Rowland, maybe? No?

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: won a drum contest sponsored by Gene Krupa at the age of 16

ctx.x: Drummer and arranger Louie Bellson is one of the most recorded musicians in jazz. He learned piano, percussion and music theory as a youth and won a drum contest sponsored by Gene Krupa at the age of 16. One year later he was playing with Benny Goodman and soon after developed the double bass drum set that has become his trademark. Louie was interviewed by Monk Rowe on April 12, 1996 at the Sarasota Jazz Festival.
